title: Lamed-He Verbs
description: Recognize the weak final radical he.

blocks.caption: Summary
blocks.html: Lamed-He verbs end in a weak he, which appears as a final vowel or drops out. בָּנָה (he built) becomes יִבְנֶה (he will build), and עָשָׂה (he made) becomes יַעֲשֶׂה. The final he is usually a spelling of a vowel that was once a full root consonant, so the ending changes across the forms.

blocks.caption: The final he
blocks.html: The final he of a Lamed-He verb is a weak letter that surfaces as a vowel: in the perfect it is -āh (בָּנָה), in the imperfect -eh (יִבְנֶה). It is not a feminine ending, even though it looks like one. Read it as the root's third radical showing through.

blocks.caption: The forms
blocks.html: The imperfect, imperative, and infinitive of these verbs end in a vowel rather than a consonant, and the class frequently overlaps with Lamed-Aleph. The perfect and imperfect endings are the main clue: -āh in the perfect, -eh in the imperfect.

blocks.caption: Common confusion
blocks.html: Do not read a final he on a verb as a feminine ending. בָּנָה is a third-person masculine perfect, not a feminine form. Compare the perfect and imperfect endings to see the weak final radical, and keep the class distinct from Lamed-Aleph, with which it overlaps.

blocks.caption: Worked example
blocks.html: Take בָּנָה ("he built") and יִבְנֶה ("he will build"). The final he is a weak letter that appears as -āh in the perfect and -eh in the imperfect. It is not a feminine ending; it is the root's third radical showing through as a vowel.

blocks.caption: Reading practice
blocks.html: Read and parse. בָּנָה הָאִישׁ — "the man built". עָשָׂה הָעָם — "the people made". The final -āh (perfect) and -eh (imperfect) are the weak final radical, not a feminine ending.
